title: Jawaharlal Nehru

cards.h: The architect of modern India's mind
cards.b: Nehru (1889-1964), the first Prime Minister (1947-64), shaped India's institutions and its political culture. Yet he is not a classical 'thinker' in the manner of Gandhi or Ambedkar, so UPSC asks about his ideas in action: democracy, secularism, socialism, planning, scientific temper and non-alignment.

Written in Ahmednagar Fort jail (1942-45) and published in 1946, The Discovery of India sees India as a palimpsest: layer upon layer of cultures, none wiped out. Unity in diversity is the central theme.

He rejects both communal history and blind Westernisation. His earlier works, Glimpses of World History (1934) and An Autobiography (1936), show a wide, humanist and Marxist-influenced outlook.

Nehru was drawn to Marxist analysis of class and imperialism but rejected violence and dictatorship. His middle path: democratic socialism, a mixed economy with a strong public sector.

Landmarks: National Planning Committee (1938), Planning Commission (1950), Industrial Policy Resolution (1956), 'socialistic pattern of society' (Avadi session, 1955), Second Plan (Mahalanobis model, heavy industry). Dams were 'the temples of modern India'.

For Nehru the state must be neutral between religions yet treat all fairly: equal respect, not hostility to religion. He opposed majority communalism more than minority communalism, as it could pose as nationalism.

He urged a scientific temper: questioning, evidence and reason. The phrase appears in Discovery of India, and now in Art. 51A(h) as a Fundamental Duty (42nd Amendment, 1976).

He saw peace and development as linked. Principles: non-alignment, anti-colonialism and anti-racism, Panchsheel (1954 agreement with China), Bandung (1955), the NAM founding (Belgrade 1961). He tried to give a newly independent India an independent voice between the two blocs.

The 1962 war with China is held up as the failure of his idealism.

• Right: favoured the Westernised elite, appeased minorities.
  • Lohia and the left: dynastic, Congress-centred and elitist, and neglected caste.
  • Swatantra: planning produced a licence-permit raj.
  • Agriculture and primary education got less priority. The Hindu rate of growth (about 3.5 per cent).
  • Defenders: built institutions, held democracy and secular state together under hard conditions.

They were close but different. Gandhi: village, decentralisation, moral politics, non-violence as creed. Nehru: modern industry, state-led growth, secular rationalism, non-violence as policy. Gandhi named Nehru his heir in 1942. Both rejected communalism and wanted an inclusive nation.

Keep the name, the year and the one-line claim ready. These three details are what examiners look for when they check a concept.

Institutions with his stamp: IITs, ISRO precursors (INCOSPAR 1962), AIIMS, CSIR, parliamentary democracy and the first Lok Sabha elections (1951-52). Contemporary debate on secularism, state versus market and foreign policy often goes back to Nehru, for or against.

Link the idea to a current event or a constitutional provision when you write. A fresh Indian example lifts a theory answer above the generic one.

"Nehru's idea of secularism was a mixture of western and Indian traditions. Discuss."
"Examine Nehru's contribution to the idea of planned development."
"Critically assess Nehru's vision of India as seen in The Discovery of India."

Structure: idea, text, five pillars, critique, Gandhi contrast, legacy.

Marks tip: open with a one-line definition, use two or three named thinkers, cases or Articles, add one Indian example, and end with a balanced, forward-looking line. Keep within the word limit.
